You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: The Next $1 Trillion Chip Company

TEXT:
1. The next $1 trillion chip company may emerge from the post-GPT era of inference accelerators, but only if it is the first to mass-produce rack-level systems and secure leading anchor customers. The current window of opportunity is narrowing, with Tenstorrent, Etched, and SambaNova expected to deliver mass-produced racks in 2026, taking the lead for now.
2. Groq and Cerebras have demonstrated that even if the architectures have flaws, as long as you have mass-produced chips at the right moment and can outperform GPUs on key metrics such as interactivity, you can achieve results at the $10 billion scale. Currently, token demand far outstrips supply, and low-latency frontier tokens are especially scarce, presenting post-GPT accelerators with a similar opportunity. However, being late by just one year comes at a high cost, and companies shipping in 2027 and beyond will face even more daunting challenges.

The next $1 trillion chip company may emerge from the post-GPT era of inference accelerators, but only if it is the first to mass-produce rack-level systems and secure leading anchor customers. The current window of opportunity is narrowing, with Tenstorrent, Etched, and SambaNova expected to deliver mass-produced racks in 2026, taking the lead for now.
I. The Next $1 Trillion Chip Company
The answer may be simpler than you think. Etched, Fractile, MatX, Positron, Rebellions, SambaNova, Tensordyne, Tenstorrent, and so on.
In the past year, two AI chip startups have achieved stunning financial results. Groq was acquired for $20 billion, and Cerebras reached a market cap of over $40 billion after its IPO. That’s substantial, but still short of the $1 trillion mark. Given today’s environment, if an inference-first system capable of running frontier models and scaling to gigawatt-level compute can expand at scale and go public, it truly stands a chance at a $1 trillion valuation.
But the architectures employed by Groq and Cerebras are not flawless. Both systems were designed before large language models went mainstream, and their early design choices don’t quite fit today’s models. I call them “pre-GPT era” accelerators.
The most well-known example, which has been widely discussed, is that they use only SRAM. Even serving a small model requires many racks of Groq; and though Cerebras’ wafer-scale marvel integrates 900,000 cores on a single chip, it still can't hold all the weights of cutting-edge models on one wafer, so it must be scaled beyond. The economics aren’t great, and the KV cache is also hard to scale smoothly—issues like this continue.
Frankly, after digging into these engineering details, I once thought these companies didn’t stand a chance in the large language model space. In fairness, who could have predicted ten years ago how large these models would become? But without high-bandwidth memory for long contexts... how can they survive? The longer the context, the better... hard to scale up, right?
The key point is, both companies had chips ready for production at the right time. No matter the shortcomings of a pure SRAM architecture, they beat GPUs on a crucial performance metric—interactivity. As Jensen so clearly demonstrated, decoding with SRAM chips opened up new possibilities for the Pareto frontier in 2026:
That’s why they achieved ten-billion-dollar results. Yeah, tens of billions of dollars—pretty crazy, right!
I used to be totally wrong in thinking their architectural limitations would stop them.
Looking back, what’s the most important thing? Timing.
When Nvidia came calling, Groq just happened to have a mass-produced product; when OpenAI engaged, Cerebras was also ready. Forget about the architectural flaws. If you can ship and establish a new Pareto frontier, good things will follow. In fact, I once thought Groq and Cerebras’ real problem was getting started too early and making design bets before the rise of the Transformer. Too early is no different than wrong...
True, an early start nearly finished them; both companies were close to running out of cash. But being early was also their only real advantage, because by the time that unforeseen inference wave arrived, they already had chips in production. Still, until Meta released Llama, both were in a default-dead posture. Llama was the first practical open-weight large language model, allowing Groq to show the world just how good an ultra-fast chatbot experience could be.
To restate: only two things matter—having a mass-produced chip at the right time and achieving a Pareto frontier that GPUs can’t match. Then, Nvidia’s Dynamo made things even better, decoupling workloads so memory-constrained decode tasks can run on SRAM chips.
II. The Post-GPT Era
[...]
If the first era of inference belonged to GPUs, then Groq and Nvidia have ushered in the next phase with GPU+LPU inference. But yet another era is coming: the post-GPT accelerator age. From matrix multiplication and interconnects to memory hierarchy, these rack-scale systems are designed from day one for large language model inference.
